content: Various pharmacological and non-pharmacological methods have been employed to suppress lactation after childbirth and alleviate associated symptoms. Despite the extensive research available, there is no universally accepted guideline for the most appropriate method to suppress lactation in postpartum women. The objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness and safety of different interventions for lactation suppression in postpartum women who have not breastfed or expressed breast milk. The goal was to identify the approach that offers the greatest benefits with the least risk. The Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register was searched up to June 30, 2012, to identify relevant studies. Randomized trials evaluating treatments for postpartum lactation suppression were included. Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the trials and extracted data. A total of 62 trials involving 6,428 women were included in the review. However, 22 of these trials did not contribute data to the meta-analyses. The included trials were generally small and of limited quality. Three trials involving 107 women demonstrated that bromocriptine significantly reduced the proportion of women who were lactating compared to no treatment within seven days postpartum. The risk ratio (RR) was 0.36, with a 95% confidence interval (CI) of 0.24 to 0.54. Seven trials that investigated estrogen preparations, including diethylstilbestrol, quinestrol, chlorotrianisene, and hexestrol, also showed a significant reduction in the proportion of lactating women compared to no treatment within seven days postpartum. The RR was 0.40, with a 95% CI of 0.29 to 0.56. No trials were identified that compared non-pharmacological methods with no treatment. Comparisons of bromocriptine with other pharmacological agents, such as methergoline, prostaglandins, pyridoxine, cabergoline, diethylstilbestrol, and cyclofenil, suggested that these treatments had similar effectiveness. Side effects were poorly reported across the trials. Importantly, no cases of thromboembolism were recorded in the four trials that specifically reported this outcome. The authors concluded that there is weak evidence suggesting that some pharmacological treatments, most of which are not currently available to the public, may be more effective than no treatment for suppressing lactation symptoms during the first postpartum week. There is no evidence to determine whether non-pharmacological approaches are more effective than no treatment. Additionally, there is insufficient evidence to evaluate the side effects of the methods used for lactation suppression. For women who desire treatment, bromocriptine may be considered in cases where it is approved for lactation suppression, provided the individual does not have a predisposition to its major side effects, which are of public concern. However, many trials did not provide data that could be included in the analyses. The authors emphasized the need for large, randomized trials to compare the effectiveness of pharmacological (particularly bromocriptine) and non-pharmacological methods with no treatment. These trials should also assess the acceptability of the interventions, address lactation symptoms that are important to women, and be adequately powered to detect clinically significant differences in major side effects between treatment groups.
